metadata.title: Machine learning procedures for predictor variable selection for schoolwork-related anxiety: evidence from PISA 2015 mathematics, reading, and science assessments

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used PISA 2015 student microdata for the United States and trimmed the dataset to retain the final sampling weight W_FSTUWT, described as the only saved weight. The analytic sample was further restricted by removing irrelevant variables, excluding specific predictor candidates (e.g., certain derived variables and variables with logical validity constraints), and applying missing-data rules (k-NN imputation after excluding the highest-missing predictors). The authors explicitly state that W_FSTUWT was used as the sampling weight in penalized regression to account for PISA’s complex sampling structure. Replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is not reported, and the paper does not describe applying replicate weights to the ML models.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 United States student data (initial N=5712), with 5593 (97.92%) completing the schoolwork-related anxiety items. The response variable ANXTEST was derived from five PISA schoolwork-related anxiety items (ST118Q01NA–ST118Q05NA). From 948 student variables, irrelevant identifiers/administration variables were removed; all derived variables were deleted except ANXTEST, and the five anxiety items were removed after deriving ANXTEST. Predictor candidates were restricted to 188 variables after excluding variables that were not suitable for modeling (e.g., OCOD1–OCOD3, ST065Class, ST125Q01) and after handling logical validity constraints by removing variables that were marked as “valid skip” when prerequisite attendance was absent (ST064, ST098, ST100, ST103, ST104, ST107). Five additional-learning hour variables (ST071Q01–ST071Q05) with the highest missing rates were excluded from subsequent analysis. Missing values for remaining predictors were imputed using k-NN with k=49 based on Gower distance for mixed data types.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (United States) schoolwork-related anxiety (ANXTEST) from ST118Q01NA–ST118Q05NA
main_findings.performance_metrics: Prediction performance (100 iterations): LASSO RMSE mean=0.866 (SD=0.014); Enet RMSE mean=0.866 (SD=0.014); Random Forest RMSE mean=0.881 (SD=0.014). Selection stability: LASSO selected ≥1 time for 187/188 predictors; ≥75 times for 79 predictors; selected in all 100 iterations for 27 predictors. LASSO vs FS agreement: 27 predictors identified by LASSO across 100 iterations; 26 also statistically significant with FS (p<0.05).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (United States) the study leveraged Gender, Want top grades (most/all), Feel like an outsider, Called on less often, and Mathematics achievement (PV) to predict schoolwork-related anxiety (ANXTEST), finding that LASSO and Elastic Net outperformed Random Forest in RMSE while producing comparable results between LASSO and Enet across 100 iterations. This indicates that penalized linear models can more reliably identify a sparse set of anxiety-related indicators from high-dimensional PISA questionnaires than nonlinear tree ensembles, supporting policy-relevant screening of students’ anxiety risk factors (while noting the study is predictive and not causal).

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzed PISA 2015 United States student data (analytic N=5593) to predict schoolwork-related anxiety (ANXTEST) derived from five PISA items (ST118Q01NA–ST118Q05NA). From 188 candidate predictors, the authors removed unsuitable variables (e.g., categories with low counts or logical “valid skip” patterns) and excluded the five additional-learning hour variables with the highest missingness before applying k-NN imputation (k=49, Gower distance). They compared LASSO, Elastic Net, and Random Forest using repeated 7:3 train/test splits with 10-fold CV for tuning and iterated the full procedure 100 times to stabilize variable-selection counts. LASSO and Enet had identical RMSE distributions (mean=0.866, SD=0.014), while Random Forest was slightly worse (mean=0.881, SD=0.014). Across iterations, 27 predictors were selected in all 100 runs, and 26 of these were also significant under forward stepwise regression (p<0.05). The paper reports sampling-weight use (W_FSTUWT) for penalized regression but does not report replicate-weight handling, and the selection counts reflect predictive association rather than causal effects.
